statement: Define an ultra as any race above 42.2 km and store race goals with the consensus descriptors (distance, elevation gain/loss, surface, altitude, continuous vs staged, support level) so rules can branch on them. 50 km is the lower bound of the ultra module.

For goals of about 100 km and longer, prioritise growing weekly running time (bounded by the athlete's history, G-1/G-2 and injury flags) ahead of pace work and ahead of lengthening the single long run; for marathon and 50 km goals keep pace work in higher proportion. Weekly volume, frequency and climbing are the training variables consistently associated with ultra performance across seven cross-sectional cohorts; the longest single run is not.
value: volume first for >=100 km; pace weighted more for <=50 km

statement: Show non-blocking readiness messages when recent weekly distance, sessions per week, or training pace look low compared with the athlete's own history and the goal, since each was associated with DNF in a 24,000-starter 56 km cohort and low volume recurs as an injury marker in trail runners. No thresholds may be hard-coded from this evidence.
value: weekly distance, sessions per week, goal pace vs recent training pace
appliesTo: Athletes 4+ weeks from an ultra goal

statement: Show an informational note, not a block, when average weekly running distance in the 12 weeks before an ultra is under 30 km. Low weekly volume is associated with injury and DNF in several cohorts (possibly reverse causation); the 30 km value comes from one 56 km cohort and is a conservative default.
appliesTo: Athletes training for 50 km and longer

statement: Display acute:chronic workload ratio only as information. Evidence conflicts (injury association above 1.5 in one study, minimal effect in another) and the load-injury relationship is non-linear, so ACWR must not hard-limit progression.

Apply conservative ramp rates and an explicit injury-history check to younger and less experienced runners, and show a note when the athlete has under 3 years of regular running before a first ultra. The 3-year value is the lower quarter of a descriptive distribution, not a risk threshold. Do not treat shorter ultra goals (about 50 km) as low-risk: entrants training for 46 km had the highest injury rate per 1000 h in one event.
appliesTo: First-time ultra and 100-mile runners; all ultra distances for the shorter-goal caution

statement: Raise the race-risk flag and recommend a more conservative pace target when forecast WBGT or temperature is high and when the runner is older than 38 (strongest for women older than 38 at 161 km). Use as a qualitative multiplier; no coefficients are available.
appliesTo: Ultra goals of 50 km to 100 miles

statement: Do not treat first-time 100-mile status as a risk factor on its own; first-timers finished more often at Western States, most likely through selection. Base caution on training data and injury history.

Include race-fuel rehearsal in long runs of ultra builds, progressing intake toward the planned race rate (ISSN range 30-50 g/h carbohydrate, 150-400 kcal/h total, shown as information with an individual-tolerance disclaimer), because nausea and GI distress are the leading cited reasons for dropping out at 161 km. Include foot-care and blister management in race readiness. Do not recommend routine NSAID use.
appliesTo: All 50 km to 100-mile builds, long runs

statement: Set race-day pacing guidance to keep heart rate at or below VT1 (aerobic zone) for most of the race (about 86% of time in this zone in a 65 km, 12 h race) and flag planned effort above VT2. For 100-mile goals use a more conservative default.
appliesTo: Ultra goals lasting 10 hours or more

statement: Estimate ultra goal times from prior ultra finishes and marathon PB first; use speed-based fitness (VO2max proxy, recent 5-10 km) for 50 to 80 km only. For 100 miles and longer, present a wide range and finish-first framing; for multi-stage events use 50-100 km race performance and last-year training speed.
value: ultra history + marathon PB; range for >=161 km
appliesTo: Goal-time estimates for 50 km to 100 miles and multi-day

statement: Include a strength-maintenance component (knee extensors and plantar flexors) in plans for about 100 km and longer trail goals. Evidence shows only that maximal isometric strength determined performance at 101 km; the dose is an engine default.
appliesTo: Athletes with 100 km or longer trail goals

statement: Use about 64 km/week (3,347 km/yr median) only as a descriptive sanity check of experienced ultrarunners' volume; never set it as a target. Strava summaries of 100-mile finishers (median peak week about 79-81 miles, about 16 h, 3-4 weeks out) are practice context only, from self-selected finishers. Cap peak volume by the athlete's own history and injury risk.

Place peak training volume about 3 weeks before the goal race (elite n = 1 structure; also the modal peak-week timing of Western States and UTMB finishers on Strava), and follow 100 km or longer races, including tune-up races, with the day-counted post-race window of H12 (hold, then 7-day steps scaled by race class). No day count is evidenced beyond the time courses cited in H12.
value: see H12: hold 7 days (100 km class) to 14 days (beyond 170 km), then 7-day steps

statement: For multi-day and stage events do not claim that pre-race volume prevents dropout; no tested pre-race variable separated finishers from non-finishers in the one cohort studied. Put risk guidance on in-event management (pacing, injury, fuel) and show 5,500 km/year only as a descriptive reference.

Do not present any longest-run length as required for, or predictive of, finishing an ultra. Finisher vs non-finisher comparisons found no significant difference (161 km, ES 0.73, P = 0.07; UTMB Strava, nearly identical medians) or lost significance after adjustment (66 km); the only positive signal is a self-reported longest run linked to faster time, not to finishing. These null results are underpowered, so they are absence of evidence, not evidence that no length matters: the rule is a copy guard (grade D) and long-run targets are sketches.
appliesTo: All ultra goals, copy and feasibility labels

statement: The D4 feasibility check works toward a longest single run Lt that is the least of the class value (180 min for 50 km, 240 min for 100 km, 240 min for 100 miles, 270 min beyond), the H2 cap and the long-run share times the larger of the class peak week and the start week, so it never exceeds the long run the plan can schedule. Back-to-backs add time on feet beyond it. These are defaults that sit at or below observed practice (every Western States finisher on Strava logged at least one 20-mile run); no study sets them.

For ultra goals, the D4 feasibility check also grows weekly running time from the start week (the larger of the typical week and the start-path floor week) toward the distance class's peak weekly time with the weekly ramp, and the label uses the slower of the long-run and weekly paths, because weekly volume and frequency, not the single long run, are the variables associated with ultra performance and DNF. The label never refuses a goal or raises load.

Cap the longest single training run at the lesser of 6 h or 60% of expected race duration; G-1 applies to both duration and distance, so the long run grows by time on feet within the 1.10x session guard even where coaching convention (for example +1 h per month) would move faster. The cap lies inside the range of named-coach conventions (3-5 h to 6-7 h) and below what finishers log when races are counted; no injury or performance study sets it, and no study links any long-run length to injury, so it is a conservative default.
unit: h; fraction of expected race duration

statement: Design intent, not implemented: one race simulation of up to 8 h per build, only within G-1, may be an entered tune-up race (50 km to 100 km); most 100-mile finishers raced during the build. It would fall no later than 3 weeks before race day and never in the taper, and after a tune-up of 100 km or more H12 applies. No code path reads h2.raceSimulationMaxHours, so the app must not describe the simulation as available. The value is a convention.
appliesTo: Ultra goals of 100 km and longer (design intent)

statement: For ultras the long run is about 45% of weekly running time (marathon and shorter 35%), always capped by H2 and G-1. The Western States peak week put about 40% of weekly distance in the long run (derived from two medians); because long runs are slower than weekday runs, the time share is higher than the distance share. Convention only.

Back-to-back long days: at most one pair every 2 weeks, in build or specific phases only, never in the taper; day 2 is no longer than day 1 (default 0.6 of day 1); the pair's combined duration is no more than 1.10x the largest 2-day total in the last 30 days (G-1 by analogy); the next day is rest or easy. No study measures back-to-backs or links them to finishing or injury; do not confuse them with same-day double sessions, which one review lists as an injury factor.
unit: weeks; ratio; ratio; fraction of day 1

statement: Apply no sex-specific long-run, back-to-back or volume values; state in rule notes that ultra training data come largely from male samples. A systematic review found sex differences in predictors and responses but evidence too weak to formulate sex-specific guidance.
